questions.q: Which of these are reasons for testing a program? Tick all that apply.
options: To make sure it produces the right output for the right input
To make sure it does not crash on unexpected input
To make sure it meets what was asked for
To find errors before users do
To make the program run faster
To reduce the number of lines of code
correct: To make sure it produces the right output for the right input
To make sure it does not crash on unexpected input
To make sure it meets what was asked for
To find errors before users do
questions.feedback: Testing finds faults. It does not make code faster or shorter.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.3 Lesson 4 — Bug hunt lab, station 1: Why test a program?

questions.q: Explain the difference between iterative testing and final testing.

markPoints.concept: iterative testing happens while the program is being written, section by section
accept: during|as it is|as you|each section|each part|throughout|as it goes|modules|bit by bit|being written|not finished|still writing|develop
markPoints.exemplar: Iterative testing happens while the program is being written, a section at a time.

markPoints.concept: final testing happens once the whole program is complete
accept: whole|complete|finished|end|all of it|everything together|once it is done
markPoints.exemplar: Final testing happens once the whole program is finished.

questions.example: Iterative testing is done while the program is being written, testing each section as it is added, so faults are found early. Final testing is done once the whole program is complete, to check that all the parts work together and that it does what was asked for.
questions.paraphrase: Iterative testing is carried out during development, checking each piece as it is built, whereas final testing comes at the end, once everything is assembled.
questions.feedback: Both halves. During, and at the end.

questions.q: Match each test data type to an example, for a program that accepts a mark between 0 and 100.
questions.feedback: Boundary data sits exactly on the limit, which is where most off-by-one faults live.

questions.q: Explain why boundary data is particularly important to test.

markPoints.concept: it sits exactly on the limit the program checks against
markPoints.exemplar: Boundary data sits exactly on the limit the program checks against.

markPoints.concept: which is where an off-by-one mistake in the condition shows up
accept: off by one|one out|mistake|mistakes|error|errors|fault|slip|wrong operator|wrong symbol|wrong sign|incorrect|missed|misses
markPoints.exemplar: So that is where a mistake in the comparison shows up, such as writing less than where less than or equal to was meant.

questions.example: Boundary data is the value right on the limit, which is exactly where a mistake in the condition shows itself — using > where >= was meant only goes wrong for the one value on the boundary, and normal data would never find it.
questions.paraphrase: Because it falls precisely on the edge of what is allowed, it is the only data that exposes an error in the comparison, such as using the wrong inequality.
questions.feedback: On the limit, and what being on the limit catches.

questions.q: A program is meant to accept a mark from 0 to 100 inclusive. What does it print when the mark entered is 100?
questions.feedback: The condition uses < where <= was meant, so the top boundary is wrongly rejected. Only boundary data finds this.
questions.hint: Try the value that sits exactly on the limit.

questions.q: Sort each fault by whether it is a syntax error or a logic error.
items: A missing colon at the end of an if line
A loop that runs one time too many
questions.feedback: A syntax error stops the program running. A logic error lets it run and produce the wrong answer, which is why it is harder to find.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.3 Lesson 4 — Bug hunt lab, station 4: Syntax errors

questions.q: Explain why a logic error is usually harder to find than a syntax error.

markPoints.concept: a syntax error is reported by the translator with a line number
accept: reports|reported|tells you|points|flagged|flags|identifies|highlights|names the line|error message|line number|will not run|refuses|stops
markPoints.exemplar: A syntax error is reported by the translator, often with a line number.

markPoints.concept: a logic error lets the program run, so nothing points to where it is
accept: runs|still works|no message|no error|nothing tells|does not stop|looks fine|seems to work|wrong answer|wrong output|wrong result
markPoints.exemplar: A logic error lets the program run, so nothing tells the programmer where to look.

questions.example: A syntax error stops the program from running at all, and the translator says which line it could not understand. A logic error breaks no rules, so the program runs happily and simply produces the wrong answer — the programmer has to work out which part of their own reasoning was wrong, with nothing pointing at it.
questions.paraphrase: The first is flagged by the translator, which names the line; the second allows the program to execute normally, so there is no message and no indication of where the fault lies.
questions.feedback: What you are told about one, and what you are not told about the other.

questions.code:
total = 0
for n in [4, 8, 15]:
    total = n
print(total)
questions.feedback: The program was meant to add the numbers up but it replaces total each time, so it ends up holding the last one. It runs perfectly: that is what makes it a logic error.
questions.hint: Read the line inside the loop carefully. Is it adding or replacing?
